**8B.10 Research Note: Fumio Kishida in 2024**

**Bottom line:** Mixed, leaning slightly toward “closer than at the start” on policy delivery and international influence, but not on durable domestic political consolidation. Kishida ended 2024 with real institutional and diplomatic gains, yet the legitimacy problem remained unresolved: approval stayed low, scandals kept dominating, and he chose to step aside rather than fight through to a strengthened end-state.

- **Title:** `Kishida’s 2024 policy speech set a broad reform-and-growth agenda` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** January 30, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html | **Summary:** At the start of the period, Kishida explicitly tied 2024 to wage growth, child support, political reform, fiscal reform, digital administration, labor reform, and defense buildup. This is the baseline program against which later progress can be judged. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.6, 8B.8

- **Title:** `Kishida apologized over the LDP funding scandal and launched reform machinery` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** January 30, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html | **Summary:** Kishida responded to the scandal with a Political Reform Headquarters, transparency pledges, and legal reform language. This is evidence that he did not simply absorb the shock passively, but tried to repair the governing coalition and preserve the broader program. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.8, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida said restoring trust in politics was the main Diet-session issue` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** June 21, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202406/21kaiken.html | **Summary:** By midyear he had already disbanded his faction, amended political-funds rules, and reported that 61 of 62 government bills had passed. That is meaningful progress on institutional control and policy throughput, even if it did not yet restore public trust. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.6, 8B.8, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida reported nearly all bills and treaties passed` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** July 3, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/actions/202407/03sei_yoto.html | **Summary:** This is one of the clearest indicators that the government could still mobilize the Diet and governing coalition to convert the agenda into concrete outputs. It supports the case that Kishida was closer to achieving the policy side of his program by the end of the period. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.6, 8B.8, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida reported concrete Japan-NATO cooperation outcomes` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** July 11, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202407/11kaiken.html | **Summary:** Japan-NATO cooperation deepened on classified information sharing, cyber, space, and support for Ukraine. This is direct evidence that his international-influence program advanced in 2024, even if it also hardened bloc politics. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.6, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida launched the Friends of the FMCT` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** September 23, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202409/23fmct.html | **Summary:** Kishida framed the FMCT initiative as a culmination of his disarmament diplomacy. That is concrete institutional and multilateral influence-building, and it is one of the strongest late-period signs of forward movement relative to the start of 2024. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.6, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida ordered disaster response with human life first` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** January 1, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/decisions/2024/0101shiji.html | **Summary:** Kishida moved quickly in the Noto earthquake response, ordering warnings, evacuation, and damage prevention. This supports the view that he managed a major domestic crisis competently, which helped preserve governing capacity. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Kishida said the government had used more than 550 billion yen in reserve funds for Noto recovery` | **Publisher:** Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | **Date:** July 1, 2024 | **URL:** https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202407/01kaiken.html | **Summary:** The cabinet turned emergency response into repeated, budgeted recovery action on infrastructure, housing, lifelines, and livelihoods. That is real implementation progress, but it is still a recovery story rather than evidence of a fully transformed domestic position. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.7, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Reuters said Kishida would step down amid scandals and rising living costs` | **Publisher:** Reuters | **Date:** August 14, 2024 | **URL:** https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japan-pm-kishida-wont-run-for-reelection-at-ldp-race-kyodo-reports-3570455 | **Summary:** Kishida’s own exit was framed as the clearest first step to show the LDP was changing. This is strong evidence against a durable power-consolidation reading: by year-end, the political base had weakened enough that controlled withdrawal was the best option. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.8, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Nippon.com reported Kishida stayed below 30% approval in August polls` | **Publisher:** Nippon.com | **Date:** August 30, 2024 | **URL:** https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-data/h30004/ | **Summary:** Public approval remained very low even after the reform push and policy outputs. That is the main reason the answer is not a clean “yes”: whatever gains he made did not translate into durable domestic legitimacy by the end of 2024. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.8, 8B.9

- **Title:** `Reuters reported real wages were still falling in spring 2024` | **Publisher:** Reuters | **Date:** May 8, 2024 | **URL:** https://www.investing.com/news/economy-indicators/japan-real-wages-fall-in-march-marking-2-years-of-decline-3430367 | **Summary:** The economic program had not yet produced a clear lived-improvement payoff for households by midyear. This matters for 8B.10 because the policy trajectory was positive, but the outcome track was still lagging under inherited inflation and currency pressure. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.7

- **Title:** `Reuters said the weak yen was hurting households and purchasing power` | **Publisher:** Reuters | **Date:** August 1, 2024 | **URL:** https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japan-warns-of-weak-yen-impact-on-households-in-government-white-paper-3551065 | **Summary:** External shocks continued to blunt Kishida’s economic message late in the year. This undercuts any strong claim that he had clearly moved the country onto a more secure domestic trajectory by the end of the period. | **QIDs:** 8B.10, 8B.7, 8B.8

**Search gap:** I did not find evidence that Kishida had materially repaired the core domestic legitimacy problem by year-end. The sources show real legislative throughput, some institutional reform, and stronger international influence, but not a restored public mandate or a durable consolidation of power.
